dora-grundlagen-01.question: What is DORA legally, and since when has it applied?

options.a: An EU directive that only applies once transposed into German law
options.b: A directly applicable EU Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2022/2554), in force since 17 January 2025
options.c: A voluntary industry self-commitment with no legal force
options.d: A purely German banking-supervision law

dora-grundlagen-01.explanation: DORA is a Regulation, not a directive - it applies directly across all EU member states without a national transposition law. Applicable since 17 Jan 2025.

dora-grundlagen-02.question: Which entities generally fall within DORA's scope?

options.a: Only credit institutions (banks)
options.b: Around 20 types of financial entities - incl. banks, payment institutions, investment firms, insurers, crypto-asset providers - plus their critical ICT third-party providers
options.c: Exclusively publicly listed companies in any industry
options.d: Only companies headquartered in Frankfurt

dora-grundlagen-02.explanation: Art. 2 DORA lists the personal scope in detail - it goes far beyond classic banks and explicitly includes ICT third-party providers.

dora-grundlagen-03.question: How does DORA account for a company's size and risk profile?

options.a: There's no difference - every requirement applies identically regardless of size
options.b: The proportionality principle scales requirements to size, risk, scale and complexity - some smaller entities may use a simplified framework
options.c: Only microenterprises must comply with DORA, large banks are exempt
options.d: Each company sets its own requirements freely

dora-grundlagen-03.explanation: Art. 4 establishes the proportionality principle; Art. 16 provides a simplified ICT risk management framework for certain smaller/less interconnected entities.

dora-grundlagen-04.question: Why do you, as an employee of a DORA-covered company, have to take training like this?

options.a: It's purely voluntary, only informally recommended by the employer
options.b: Art. 13(6) DORA requires financial entities to make ICT security awareness programmes and digital operational resilience training a compulsory part of staff training schemes for ALL employees and senior management
options.c: Only IT staff need to be trained, everyone else is exempt
options.d: The training duty applies only to senior management members, not regular staff

dora-grundlagen-04.explanation: Unlike NIS2 (which only mandates training for management bodies), DORA Art. 13(6) explicitly requires training for ALL staff AND senior management - with complexity matched to each person's role.

dora-risikomanagement-01.question: Under DORA, who bears ultimate responsibility for a financial entity's ICT risk management?

options.a: Exclusively the IT department
options.b: The management body (executive/supervisory board) - this responsibility cannot be outsourced
options.c: The external ICT third-party provider
options.d: The national supervisory authority itself

dora-risikomanagement-01.explanation: Art. 5 makes clear the management body bears ultimate responsibility and cannot delegate it away, even where operational tasks are delegated.

dora-risikomanagement-02.question: What core functions must the ICT risk management framework cover under DORA?

options.a: Only customer-data encryption
options.b: Identification, protection/prevention, detection, response/recovery, and learning/evolving in handling ICT risk
options.c: Exclusively the annual financial audit
options.d: Only the selection of a cloud provider

dora-risikomanagement-02.explanation: Art. 6-14 structure the framework along these functions - a scheme similar to the well-known identify-protect-detect-respond-recover cycle.

dora-risikomanagement-03.question: How often must the ICT risk management framework be reviewed at minimum?

options.a: Only once, when first introduced
options.b: At least once a year, plus after major ICT incidents or significant changes
options.c: Every 10 years
options.d: A review isn't required at all

dora-risikomanagement-03.explanation: Art. 6(5) requires at least an annual review, additionally triggered by major incidents or significant changes.

dora-risikomanagement-04.question: What does DORA require regarding backup policies and disaster recovery?

options.a: Entities must establish and regularly test backup policies, recovery procedures, and business continuity plans for critical/important functions
options.b: Backups are explicitly not required under DORA
options.c: Only physical paper documents need to be backed up
options.d: Backup duties only apply to companies outside the EU

dora-risikomanagement-04.explanation: Art. 11-12 require documented backup policies, recovery procedures, and business continuity plans that must be tested regularly.

dora-meldepflichten-01.question: What criteria determine whether an ICT incident is classified as 'major'?

options.a: Solely the IT lead's personal judgment
options.b: Among others: number of clients/counterparts affected, duration and downtime, geographic spread, data losses, and economic/reputational impact
options.c: Solely the number of staff involved
options.d: There are no defined criteria

dora-meldepflichten-01.explanation: Art. 18 DORA together with RTS (EU) 2024/1772 sets out concrete, multi-dimensional classification criteria, not a single metric.

dora-meldepflichten-02.question: Within what timeframe must a major ICT incident first be reported to the competent authority?

options.a: Within 4 hours of classification as major
options.b: Only at year-end in the annual report
options.c: There is no reporting deadline, only a recommendation
options.d: Within 30 days of the incident

dora-meldepflichten-02.explanation: The clock starts at classification, not detection - though classification itself should happen without undue delay (commonly cited as roughly 24 hours after detection in practice). REVIEW NOTE: this deadline is flagged Tier C (secondary-source only) in the pre-review dossier - verify against the primary text of RTS (EU) 2025/301 before use.

dora-meldepflichten-03.question: What happens after the initial notification of a major ICT incident?

options.a: An intermediate report follows within 72 hours of classification, and a final report within one month of the intermediate report
options.b: The initial notification already satisfies all reporting duties
options.c: Only a summary report after 5 years follows
options.d: An intermediate report is only required for cyberattacks, not other ICT incidents

dora-meldepflichten-03.explanation: The three-stage reporting cascade (initial, intermediate, final) is a core mechanism of Art. 19. REVIEW NOTE: see the Tier C note on meldepflichten-02, same sourcing situation.

dora-meldepflichten-04.question: Who receives major ICT incident reports, and what applies to significant cyber threats that haven't (yet) become an incident?

options.a: Exclusively the press, to warn customers
options.b: The competent national supervisory authority (e.g. BaFin); significant cyber threats may additionally be reported voluntarily
options.c: Only the entity's own supervisory board, never an external authority
options.d: Reports are by design anonymous with no designated recipient

dora-meldepflichten-04.explanation: Reports go to the competent authority (in Germany, typically BaFin); Art. 19(2) additionally opens a voluntary reporting channel for significant cyber threats.

dora-testing-01.question: How often must financial entities (other than microenterprises) at minimum test the ICT systems supporting critical or important functions?

options.a: At least once a year
options.b: Only once, when a system is first deployed
options.c: Every 10 years
options.d: Testing duties only apply to cloud systems

dora-testing-01.explanation: Art. 24 requires a comprehensive, risk-based testing programme with at least yearly tests for critical/important functions.

dora-testing-02.question: What is threat-led penetration testing (TLPT) under DORA, and who must perform it?

options.a: A simple automated virus scan every company must run weekly
options.b: A realistic, coordinated advanced test mandatory only for entities specifically designated by the competent authority (typically large, systemically important ones)
options.c: A test only the European Central Bank runs on itself
options.d: A test mandatory for every DORA-covered entity without exception

dora-testing-02.explanation: TLPT is not a standard test for everyone, but a targeted, supervisor-coordinated exercise for specifically designated entities.

dora-testing-03.question: At what minimum interval must designated entities perform a TLPT?

options.a: At least every 3 years
options.b: Only once, at company founding
options.c: Daily
options.d: Every 20 years

dora-testing-03.explanation: Art. 26(1) sets a minimum 3-year interval; the competent authority may require more frequent testing case by case.

dora-testing-04.question: What requirement applies to who performs ICT resilience tests under DORA?

options.a: Tests may only be performed by the CEO personally
options.b: They must be performed by independent parties - internal testers with dedicated resources and no conflicts of interest, or external auditors
options.c: Tests may only be performed by the entity's own competitors
options.d: Independence is not required under DORA

dora-testing-04.explanation: Art. 24-25 require independent testing to avoid conflicts of interest and self-review.

dora-drittparteien-01.question: What must financial entities maintain and keep current regarding their ICT third-party providers?

options.a: Nothing at all - third-party relationships aren't subject to a documentation duty
options.b: A Register of Information covering all contractual arrangements with ICT third-party providers
options.c: Only a verbal list that doesn't need to be documented
options.d: A register only for providers based outside the EU

dora-drittparteien-01.explanation: Art. 28(3) requires an up-to-date register of all ICT third-party contracts - a central basis for supervisory oversight.

dora-drittparteien-02.question: What elements must contracts with ICT third-party providers include at minimum under DORA?

options.a: Only the price of the service
options.b: Among others: a clear service description, audit rights, sub-outsourcing conditions, and exit strategies
options.c: Contract duration is irrelevant under DORA
options.d: Exclusively a confidentiality clause, all other content is optional

dora-drittparteien-02.explanation: Art. 30 sets binding minimum contract contents for ICT third-party contracts, specifically to ensure exit capability and control rights.

dora-drittparteien-03.question: What happens when an ICT third-party provider is designated 'critical' (CTPP)?

options.a: It's subject to no additional oversight
options.b: It becomes subject to direct EU-level oversight by one of the European Supervisory Authorities acting as Lead Overseer
options.c: It's automatically barred from being used by financial entities
options.d: Only non-EU national authorities may oversee it

dora-drittparteien-03.explanation: Art. 31-44 establish a dedicated oversight framework for critical ICT third-party providers, with direct supervision by one of the three ESAs.

dora-drittparteien-04.question: Why is ICT third-party concentration risk relevant for financial entities under DORA?

options.a: It's irrelevant, DORA doesn't address this topic
options.b: Over-reliance on a small number of (especially critical) ICT providers can pose a systemic risk to the financial sector and must be factored into risk assessment
options.c: Concentration risk only applies to equity portfolios, not IT service providers
options.d: Only providers with fewer than 10 employees count as concentration risk

dora-drittparteien-04.explanation: DORA explicitly addresses the systemic risk that arises when a large share of the financial sector depends on the same small set of ICT providers.
